title: Major burns
subtitle: Airway, area, fluids, transfer

sources.title: ISBI practice guidelines for burn care

sources.org: American College of Surgeons Committee on Trauma
sources.title: Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) Student Course Manual

red_flags.text: Facial burns, singed nasal hair, soot in the mouth, hoarseness or stridor. The airway will swell.
Burn sustained in an enclosed space, or any reduced conscious level: assume carbon monoxide or cyanide exposure.
Circumferential full-thickness burn of a limb, or of the chest with rising airway pressures.
High-voltage electrical injury: the surface burn understates the deep muscle damage.
Chemical burn still in contact with the skin, or a burn with an inconsistent history in a child or vulnerable adult.

do_now.text: Stop the burning process, remove clothing and jewellery, and irrigate a chemical burn with running water for a prolonged period.
Assess the airway first and intubate early if there is any inhalational feature. The window closes as oedema develops.
High-flow oxygen for every significant burn, and specifically for suspected carbon monoxide exposure.
Cool the burn with running water for about 20 minutes within the first three hours, then keep the patient warm. Cool the burn, warm the patient.

assess.text: Estimate burn surface area excluding simple erythema, then check it against a chart rather than an impression.
Assess depth by capillary refill, sensation and appearance, and accept that depth declares itself over 48 hours.
Full trauma survey: a burn is often accompanied by a fall, a blast or an inhalation injury.
Weigh the patient or obtain an accurate weight. Every fluid calculation depends on it.
Document the mechanism, the time of injury and the pre-hospital fluid. Resuscitation is timed from the burn, not from arrival.

investigate.text: Arterial gas with carboxyhaemoglobin and lactate. A high lactate with a normal gas suggests cyanide toxicity.
FBC, U&E, creatine kinase, myoglobin and urinalysis for electrical or extensive deep burns.
Chest radiograph and, where indicated, bronchoscopy for inhalational injury.
Hourly urine output is the resuscitation monitor. It is more useful than any single blood test.
ECG and cardiac monitoring after high-voltage electrical injury.

resuscitate.text: Start formal fluid resuscitation for adults above roughly 15 percent total body surface area, and children above roughly 10 percent, using a weight and area formula.
Titrate to urine output, not to the formula. The formula is a starting rate that is expected to change.
Avoid over-resuscitation. Fluid creep causes compartment syndrome, pulmonary oedema and a worse outcome than modest under-resuscitation.
Analgesia intravenously, titrated. Intramuscular absorption is unreliable in a shocked burned patient.
Early enteral feeding and active warming. Tetanus status checked and updated.

definitive.text: Escharotomy for a circumferential full-thickness burn threatening limb perfusion or ventilation.
Dress with a clean non-adherent dressing and transfer. Definitive debridement and grafting belong to the burns unit.
Prophylactic systemic antibiotics are not indicated for a fresh burn. Treat infection when it appears.
Early excision and grafting of deep burns, planned by the burns service.

escalate.text: Refer to a burns unit for a large area burn, any full-thickness burn, burns of face, hands, feet, perineum or major joints, circumferential burns, inhalational, electrical or chemical injury, and burns at the extremes of age.
Speak to the burns unit before dressing, and follow their dressing instruction: an inappropriate dressing makes assessment on arrival harder.
Safeguarding referral for any burn with an inconsistent history, a delayed presentation, or a pattern suggesting non-accidental injury.

notes: The three decisions in the first hour are the airway, the surface area, and whether this patient is being transferred.
Cool the burn, warm the patient. Both halves are frequently got wrong at the same time.
Erythema is not included in surface area, and including it is the commonest reason for over-resuscitation.
